title: Massachusetts v. EPA (2007)
summary: Massachusetts had standing to challenge EPA’s denial of a greenhouse-gas rulemaking petition. EPA possessed statutory authority and had to justify its response through the Clean Air Act’s criteria; the Court reversed and remanded without ordering particular regulations.
notes: The vote was 5-4 with Justice Stevens writing; a divided D.C. Circuit panel had ruled for EPA. Chief Justice Roberts dissented on standing (joined by Scalia, Thomas and Alito), and Justice Scalia dissented on the merits (joined by Roberts, Thomas and Alito).

sections.Parties: Private organizations petitioned the Environmental Protection Agency to regulate greenhouse-gas emissions from new motor vehicles. Massachusetts, other states, and additional petitioners sought judicial review after EPA denied the petition. The Court needed one petitioner with standing and focused on Massachusetts. EPA defended both its refusal to regulate and its objection to the petitioners’ standing.
sections.Material Facts:
The state relied on threatened and existing loss of coastal property as sea levels rose. Its submissions connected greenhouse gases to warming and coastal inundation; it also emphasized state-owned land. EPA argued that the requested regulation would affect too small a portion of worldwide emissions and that increases elsewhere would overwhelm any reduction. The majority relied on uncontested affidavits and recognized that regulation could reduce risk even if it could not eliminate global warming.

EPA sought comments and considered a National Research Council report, then denied the petition on two grounds. It claimed the Clean Air Act did not authorize greenhouse-gas regulation and, alternatively, that regulation was unwise because of scientific uncertainty, existing voluntary programs, effects on foreign negotiations, and a preference for a broader response. It also argued that emissions regulation would intrude on the Transportation Department’s fuel-economy responsibilities.
sections.Procedural History: EPA denied the rulemaking petition in 2003 after receiving extensive public comment. The petitioners sought review in the D.C. Circuit under the Clean Air Act’s judicial-review provision. The Supreme Court held that Massachusetts had standing, rejected EPA’s statutory and policy grounds for the denial, and reversed and remanded. The assigned course materials reproduce the merits discussion at printed pages1068–1077 and the standing discussion at1230–1243; the excerpts do not provide a complete account of every lower-court opinion.
sections.Issue:
Whether Massachusetts showed a concrete and particularized injury sufficiently traceable to EPA’s refusal and redressable by the requested reconsideration and regulation, considering its state status and statutory procedural right.

Did the Act authorize EPA to regulate these gases, and were the reasons for refusing to exercise its judgment consistent with the statute?
sections.Holding:
Massachusetts had standing to challenge denial of the rulemaking petition. Its territorial and property interests, procedural right, and the possibility of reducing the risk supplied the required stake. The majority’s special-solicitude analysis did not announce that every state objection to federal policy is justiciable.

Greenhouse gases fell within the Act’s broad definition of air pollutant, and EPA possessed regulatory authority under § 202(a)(1). The offered reasons did not justify refusal to make the judgment the statute required. The Court remanded without ordering an endangerment finding or specifying the eventual regulations.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority reasoned that joining the Union displaced some state powers to protect against external harms and placed responsibilities in the federal government. A procedural right to challenge EPA’s denial and a concrete coastal interest therefore supported special solicitude. Widespread climate effects did not erase particular injury to state-owned land. Domestic motor-vehicle emissions made a meaningful contribution to the problem, and incremental reduction could improve Massachusetts’s position despite foreign emissions. Roberts, joined by Scalia, Thomas, and Alito, rejected relaxing Article III for states and criticized the evidence connecting a particular regulatory step to prevention of particular land loss. The editors identify several possible understandings of the majority and question the breadth of its procedural-right account. Later assigned notes apply ordinary limits to state suits and distinguish enforcement discretion in United States v. Texas. Those qualifications belong alongside the holding.

The statutory definition included physical and chemical substances entering ambient air. Later congressional research measures and failed legislative proposals did not withdraw that authority. Brown & Williamson was distinguishable because greenhouse-gas regulation did not require a product ban or contradict a tobacco-like scheme of later enactments. EPA’s environmental responsibility could coexist with the Transportation Department’s fuel-economy role. A denial of a rulemaking petition differed from a refusal to enforce: petitions receive formal treatment and explanation and often raise legal questions, though review remains limited and deferential. The agency’s judgment had to concern the statutory endangerment inquiry. General policy preferences and diplomatic considerations did not explain refusing that inquiry; profound scientific uncertainty could matter only through a reasoned explanation. Scalia, joined by Roberts, Thomas, and Alito, argued that the statute left discretion when to form a judgment, that EPA had explained uncertainty, and that deference supported its interpretation. That dissent’s Chevron argument is part of the 2007 account, not a statement of current Chevron doctrine.

topics.lrs-n-rulemaking-petitions: The denial of a rulemaking petition received review, and EPA’s reasons had to address the criteria in its authorizing statute.
topics.lrs-n-nonreviewability: The Court distinguished rulemaking-petition denials from enforcement refusals under Chaney.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The Court rejected reasons disconnected from the statutory endangerment inquiry and remanded without dictating a finding.
topics.lrs-n-organic-statute-factors: EPA had to ground its response in the Clean Air Act’s endangerment criteria; unrelated voluntary-program and diplomatic preferences could not justify refusing that inquiry. The Court left the endangerment finding and the role of policy after such a finding undecided.
topics.lrs-n-standing-state: The majority combines state status, territory, and a review right; later notes limit extrapolation.
topics.lrs-n-standing-causation: Incremental emissions reduction can reduce an identified risk without solving the entire global problem.
topics.lrs-n-standing-procedure: The opinion invokes a procedural right; editorial notes question how broadly to read it.
topics.lrs-i-major-questions: EPA relied on Brown & Williamson to deny authority over greenhouse gases and the Court distinguished it, a key data point for later major-questions analysis.
